items.prompt: Which is the primary source for the exam date?
choices: A classmate's forwarded screenshot
The teacher's posted schedule
The group chat's most-liked reply
items.explanation: The posted schedule is the original; the screenshot and the reply both repeat it.

items.prompt: A friend retells what a news article said. Is the friend a primary or secondary source for the article's content?
choices: Secondary, because they are repeating it
Primary, because they read it themselves
Neither, because retelling is only gossip
items.explanation: Anyone describing or repeating the original is a secondary source for it.

items.prompt: Which best describes a secondary source?
choices: Something that is always less accurate than the original
Something published after the year 2000
Something that repeats or summarizes an original
items.explanation: Secondary means it comes from the original, not that it is wrong or new.

items.prompt: A recipe's author cooked the dish and wrote down what they did. For that cooking, the author is a...
choices: Secondary source of their own cooking
Primary source of their own cooking
Neither kind of source at all
items.explanation: The person who did the thing is the original source of what they did.

items.prompt: Is a secondary source always worse than a primary one?
choices: No, it is often faster and good enough
Yes, because it can never be accurate
Yes, because it is always out of date
items.explanation: They fail in different ways; a summary can be fine for low-stakes use.

items.prompt: What is the point of a primary source in a rumor?
choices: It makes the rumor spread more quickly
It proves the people repeating it are honest
It can settle the claim at its origin
items.explanation: Going to the original lets you check the claim itself, not people's reports of it.

items.prompt: Each extra layer between you and the original mainly adds...
choices: A guarantee that every error gets caught early
A chance for detail to be lost or changed
More people who have checked the claim
items.explanation: Summarizing loses precision, and later layers tend to copy earlier ones.

items.prompt: A classmate says 'the teacher told me, here is a photo of the page.' The photo is...
choices: A secondary copy of the original schedule
The primary source, since it shows the page
A proof that the schedule has changed
items.explanation: A photo is a copy; the original is the page itself, which may have changed since.

items.prompt: Your sister says a store's sale ends Sunday and shows you the store's own sale poster photographed that morning. What is the best description of what you hold?
choices: A primary source, since the poster is shown in the photo
A secondary copy of a primary source you can still check
Unverifiable gossip, since no one checked the actual store
A weak source, since photos are always out of date
items.explanation: The photo copies the poster; the store's own listing is the original you can still go and check.
items.reference:
Original versus copy
🏫 Primary: the teacher's posted schedule
📱 Secondary: a screenshot or retelling of it
🔗 Check: can you reach the original yourself?
Why: a primary source is the original that can settle the claim; a secondary source describes or repeats it.
items.learnMore:
Primary and secondary sources

A primary source is the original place a claim can be settled. A secondary source reports, summarizes or repeats it. Neither is better in general, but each extra layer is a chance to drop or change a detail.

Common mistake

Thinking a screenshot of an official page is itself the official page.
items.reflection: Think of a piece of news you heard last week. Could you name the original place it came from, or only the person who told you?

items.prompt: Two websites both explain the same rule, and one of them quotes and links the official rulebook. Which statement about them is most accurate?
choices: The rulebook is primary; both websites are secondary
Both are primary, since both explain the rule well
The linking website is primary, since it quotes directly
Neither is useful until their authors are named
items.explanation: The rulebook is the origin; any page explaining it, even with a quote and link, is a secondary description of it.

The footage and the coach are both equally secondary sources
The footage is secondary, since it was recorded afterward
The coach is secondary; the footage is closer to primary
items.explanation: Recording the event itself is nearer the original than someone's account of it, though the full original is the match.

items.prompt: Three classmates forward one screenshot. How many independent claims is that?
choices: Three claims, one per person
Zero claims, because it is a rumor
One claim, copied twice
items.explanation: Only the first poster started a claim; the forwards add nothing new.

items.prompt: What makes agreement real corroboration?
choices: The reports use exactly the same words
The reports come from different origins
The reports came from the most-liked posts
items.explanation: Independence is what makes a second report count as extra support.

items.prompt: A second report agrees but copies the first word for word. It is...
choices: The same claim passed along again
Strong support for the first claim
Proof that the first claim is false
items.explanation: Copying creates agreement without creating a second check.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest kind of corroboration?
choices: Many people sharing one message
A popular page repeating the claim
Two people who each checked the original
items.explanation: Separate people who each went to the original give independent confirmation.

items.prompt: A rumor appears on five sites that all cite one blog post. How many origins is that?
choices: Five, one for each website
One, the blog post they all cite
None, since blogs do not count
items.explanation: All five trace back to the same post.

items.prompt: A fourth classmate says her older sister, who is in the class, heard it from the teacher. This is...
choices: A separate arrow worth weighing
The same claim as the other three
Automatically proof the rumor is true
items.explanation: A named, plausibly informed, separate source starts a new line of information, though it can still be wrong.

items.prompt: Why can a wrong claim look well supported?
choices: Wrong claims are repeated less than true ones
Sources never copy each other's mistakes
Many sources can repeat the same error
items.explanation: An early mistake gets copied forward, so the count grows without any new checking.

items.prompt: In the interactive model, 10 sources that all copied each other give about the same confidence as...
choices: Ten independent checks
A single independent check
Zero checks of any kind
items.explanation: The model counts independent checks, not sources, so ten copies still count as one.

items.prompt: Four news pages report the same statistic. Page A links the original report; B, C and D each cite page A. Roughly how many independent confirmations of the statistic exist?
choices: Four, one for every page that reports it
One, the original report all four rest on
Three, since B, C and D all agree
Two, the original and the page that links it
items.explanation: B, C and D inherit from A, which inherits from the report, so the origin count is one.
items.reference:
Count origins, not voices
🗣️ Three people say it
🔁 Two of them forwarded the first one
1️⃣ Independent claims: one
Why: agreement only counts as support if the reports start from different origins.
items.learnMore:
The corroboration trap

Many sources agreeing is weak evidence when they all trace back to one original claim. Real corroboration means reports that start from different origins, each of which did its own checking.

Common mistake

Counting how many people repeat a claim instead of asking where each got it.
items.reflection: Recall a time several people told you the same thing. Did they each find out separately, or did it pass from one person to the next?

items.prompt: A group chat has eight people saying a shop is closing. One says 'I walked past, the windows were papered over'; the other seven say 'heard it from the chat'. How should the claim be weighed?
choices: As one real observation plus seven repeats of the chat
As eight separate reports, each adding the same support
As false, since seven people never saw it
As unknowable until all eight people are asked
items.explanation: Only the person who walked past is an independent origin; the rest repeat the chat.

A post that was shared across many different groups

items.explanation: Independent checks of the original raise confidence; reach and polish do not.

items.explanation: Copies of a claim do not re-check it, so silence does not show anyone verified it.

items.prompt: Which credibility signal is the strongest?
choices: Matches the primary source
Looks professionally designed
Is repeated by many accounts
items.explanation: Checking the claim against the original is the check itself.

items.prompt: Which signal is the weakest?
choices: The author has relevant standing
It links the primary source
It looks polished and well written
items.explanation: Polish is unrelated to whether anyone checked the claim.

items.prompt: A forwarded screenshot has the school's logo. That tells you...
choices: That the school wrote the screenshot
Very little about whether it is true
That the claim was checked against the schedule
items.explanation: A logo is easy to copy and says nothing about verification.

items.prompt: Why are the weakest signals risky?
choices: They are the easiest ones to notice
They are the hardest ones to notice
They only appear on very old pages
items.explanation: They are visible at a glance, so they stand in for checking.

items.prompt: A link that lets you open the original counts as...
choices: A weak signal, since links can often be wrong
No signal, since anyone can add links
A strong signal, since you can verify it
items.explanation: A checkable link means you can do the check yourself.

items.prompt: Expertise of the author is best described as...
choices: Proof that this exact claim is true
A reason to raise the odds a little
A reason to skip checking entirely
items.explanation: Standing shifts the probability but does not prove a specific claim.

items.prompt: A bus timetable page and a multiplication table page are both a year old. Which is the bigger worry?
choices: The bus timetable page
The multiplication table page
Neither is a worry at all
items.explanation: Timetables change often; multiplication tables do not.

items.prompt: A five-year-old explanation of how the multiplication table works is...
choices: Probably out of date
Impossible to judge at all
Probably still correct
items.explanation: That topic does not change, so age is not a red flag.

items.prompt: Two pages give different deadlines for a form. Page one is polished and has many shares; page two is plain but links the official notice, and its dates match the notice. Which should you trust?
choices: Page one, since many shares suggest it was checked
Page two, since it matches the official notice
Neither, since both could be copies of each other
Page one, since polish suggests the author is careful
items.explanation: Matching the primary source outranks polish and share counts.
items.reference:
Strongest to weakest
✅ Matches the primary source
🔗 Links the primary source
🧑‍🏫 Author with relevant standing
🔁 Many repeat it
🎨 Looks polished
Why: signals that need no checking are easy to notice but predict accuracy least.
items.learnMore:
Ranking credibility signals

The strongest signal is that the claim matches the primary source. A checkable link comes next, then author standing. Repetition and polish are weak, though they are the easiest to notice.

Common mistake

Trusting a page because it looks professional or has a school logo.
items.reflection: Think of the last page that felt trustworthy to you. Which signals did you actually check, and which only felt convincing?

items.prompt: A claim comes from a well-known doctor but cites nothing and gives no way to check it. How does the author's standing affect the claim?
choices: It raises the odds, but the claim is still unchecked
It makes the claim certain, since doctors are trained
It makes no difference, since doctors can be wrong
It makes the claim false until a source is shown
items.explanation: Expertise is a reasonable prior, not a substitute for checking when the stakes justify it.

choices: The number of classmates repeating it
The teacher's posted schedule
The wording of the original post
items.explanation: The primary source can settle the claim in minutes.

items.prompt: The cafeteria is serving pizza today, says a classmate. Best response?
choices: Shallow trust; you will see when you arrive
Trace it back to the cafeteria's kitchen staff
Refuse to believe it until two others agree
items.explanation: Wrong costs little and corrects itself on arrival.

items.prompt: Which claim deserves the most checking?
choices: What flavor the snack at school will be this week
Which classmate sits near the window
Whether tonight is your only study night
items.explanation: It feeds a real decision that is hard to undo by morning.

items.prompt: What does 'easily reversible' mean here?
choices: The claim has been repeated many times
You can correct a wrong choice cheaply
The source is older than a year
items.explanation: Easy to undo means mistakes cost little.

items.prompt: Step one of tracing a claim is to check...
choices: Whether the repeaters are independent
How polished the screenshot looks
How many reactions the post has
items.explanation: Independence tells you if the count means anything.

items.prompt: After finding the course page says Monday, what is a sensible next step?
choices: Ignore the page and trust the chat
Forward the rumor to more classmates
Message the teacher to confirm directly
items.explanation: The page may lag a change, so confirm with the teacher.

items.prompt: Do you need to find who the unnamed older student was?
choices: Yes, or the check is not valid
No, tracing to the course page is enough
Yes, and then ask them to prove it
items.explanation: Checking the primary source resolves the question without identifying the origin.

items.prompt: A rule of thumb for effort is to spend more when being wrong...
choices: Is costly or hard to undo
Is cheap and quickly fixed
Is about a topic you like
items.explanation: Stakes and reversibility set the effort.

items.prompt: You see a post saying a bridge on your route is closed tomorrow. A detour would add ten minutes; checking the transport authority's page takes one. What is the best move?
choices: Trust the post, since ten minutes is not much
Check the page; a minute beats a wasted trip
Ask three friends, since agreement is enough proof
Ignore it, since most such posts are wrong
items.explanation: A one-minute check is cheap compared with a possibly wasted trip.
items.reference:
Match effort to stakes
🍕 Cafeteria menu: low cost, easy fix, trust it
📚 Exam night: moderate cost, trace it
💊 Child's treatment: high cost, trace it fully
Why: the cost of checking should be weighed against the cost of being wrong and how reversible it is.
items.learnMore:
Calibrating verification

Tracing everything is impractical. The effort should grow with the stakes and shrink with how easily a mistake can be undone. Low-stakes, easily reversed claims deserve shallow trust.

Common mistake

Applying the same depth of checking to every claim, or to none.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you made on an unchecked claim. Looking back, was the effort you spent matched to what was at stake?

items.explanation: A wrong guess about a biscuit is cheap and corrected on arrival; the others carry real costs.

items.prompt: A study tested a supplement on adults. A post says it helps kids. This is...
choices: Fine, since adults and kids are alike
A confirmation of the study's results
A claim stretched past what was tested
items.explanation: The study did not test children.

items.prompt: Which detail belongs to a study's boundaries?
choices: How many people shared its summary
Who was studied and for how long
How polished its website looks
items.explanation: Participants, duration, method and outcome define the boundaries.

items.prompt: A blog names a journal but gives no link. Is it easy to check?
choices: No, the reader must search for the paper
Yes, the name alone is enough
Yes, journals are always listed first
items.explanation: A named journal without a link still leaves the tracing to you.

items.prompt: If a post cites a blog that cites a blog that cites a study, how many secondary layers are there?
choices: One layer, the closest blog
None, since all are 'sources'
Two layers before the study
items.explanation: Two blogs sit between the reader and the study.

items.prompt: What should you compare to catch a stretched claim?
choices: The post's date and today's date
The post's claim and the study's tested scope
The number of likes on the post and the study's authors
items.explanation: The mismatch between the claim and what was tested is the gap.

items.prompt: A study ran twelve weeks. A post claims a result 'within a week'. Is that supported?
choices: Not by this study, which ran longer
Yes, because twelve is more than one
Yes, results always appear early
items.explanation: The study never reported what happens in a week.

items.prompt: Before changing a child's prescribed treatment based on a post, whom should you consult?
choices: The neighbor who shared the post
The group chat that sent the post
The child's actual doctor
items.explanation: Bring the traced mismatch to the clinician who knows the case.

items.prompt: Does 'a pediatrician recommended it' settle the claim?
choices: Yes, doctors are always right
No, it does not replace checking it
Yes, if three families agree
items.explanation: The messenger's credibility is a prior, not proof.

items.prompt: A headline says 'Study proves a new tea lowers anxiety in teenagers.' The paper tested forty adults over ages 40 to 60 for two weeks. What is the most accurate summary of the headline?
choices: Supported, since anxiety is similar at all ages
Stretched: the study tested older adults for two weeks
Supported, since a tea study counts for every group of people
Fabricated, since no study could exist on tea
items.explanation: The headline claims teenagers; the paper tested a different group.
items.reference:
Claim versus study
👥 Who: adults with a diagnosed deficiency
⏱️ How long: twelve weeks
🩺 Setting: medical supervision
⚠️ Post says: kids, a week, instead of treatment
Why: a study supports only the people, duration and method it actually tested.
items.learnMore:
Claims stretched beyond a source

A study has boundaries: who was studied, for how long, with what method, measuring what. A post can say 'based on a study' while claiming something broader than the study tested.

Common mistake

Assuming a link or a citation means the source says what the post says.
items.reflection: Think of a headline you read that seemed bigger than its details. What would you need to open to see what was actually tested?

Does it prove the app would help the post's readers?
items.explanation: Who was studied limits who the result applies to; the claim extends to everyone.

Why: a study supports only the people, duration and method it actually tested.
items.learnMore:
Claims stretched beyond a source

A study has boundaries: who was studied, for how long, with what method, measuring what. A post can say 'based on a study' while claiming something broader than the study tested.

Common mistake

Assuming a link or a citation means the source says what the post says.
items.reflection: Think of a headline you read that seemed bigger than its details. What would you need to open to see what was actually tested?

choices: Share the finding quickly to warn everyone around
Repeat the original post with a note saying 'maybe'
